title: SpaceX’s Starship Soars to Orbit for First Time on Sept. 28 – Watch Live!
body:
The world’s most powerful launch vehicle is set to make history on Monday, September 28, when SpaceX will attempt the first orbital flight of its Starship megarocket from the company’s Boca Chica, Texas, site. Liftoff is slated for 8:15 a.m. EDT (12:15 GMT), and the event will be streamed live, offering a front‑row seat to a test that could reshape access to space for both government and commercial customers.

Starship, a fully reusable two‑stage system composed of the Super Heavy booster and the Starship spacecraft, represents a dramatic departure from conventional launch architecture. At an estimated 5,000 tonnes of thrust at liftoak, Super Heavy dwarfs the power of any operational rocket today, while the Starship upper stage is designed to carry payloads — and eventually crews — to low‑Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, and beyond. If the test succeeds, SpaceX will have demonstrated the vehicle’s ability to lift off, separate, and achieve a stable orbit, clearing a major technical hurdle that has so far limited the system to sub‑orbital hops and high‑altitude flight tests.

The upcoming flight follows a series of incremental milestones that have gradually expanded the vehicle’s capabilities. Earlier this year, Starship performed a successful high‑altitude test, reaching roughly 10 km before executing a controlled “flip‑over” maneuver and a soft landing that, while not perfect, proved the vehicle’s aerodynamic control and re‑entry systems. Subsequent static‑fire tests of the Super Heavy booster have validated the performance of its 33 Raptor engines, each delivering about 2 MN of thrust. The current launch will be the first time the full stack – Super Heavy and Starship – is fired together, and it will be the inaugural attempt to achieve orbital velocity, roughly 7.8 km/s.

Beyond the engineering triumph, the flight carries significant commercial and strategic implications. NASA’s Artemis program has selected a version of Starship as the lander that will ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface, a contract that hinges on the vehicle’s ability to reach orbit reliably. Meanwhile, SpaceX’s own satellite constellation, Starlink, could eventually be deployed using Starship’s massive payload capacity, reducing launch costs per kilogram and accelerating the rollout of broadband services worldwide. The megarocket also promises to open new possibilities for deep‑space missions, including crewed voyages to Mars that Elon Musk has long championed as a cornerstone of humanity’s multi‑planetary future.

Nevertheless, the test is not without risk. The sheer scale of the vehicle introduces complex aerodynamic, structural, and thermal challenges, and a failure at any stage—ignition, stage separation, or orbital insertion—could result in the loss of the vehicle. SpaceX has built a robust telemetry and safety infrastructure, and the Boca Chica launch pad has been reinforced with a massive “launch tower” and flame‑deflection systems to protect the surrounding area. The company has also prepared contingency plans, including a remote‑controlled shutdown if the vehicle deviates from its intended trajectory. Observers will be watching closely not only for success but for the data that can be harvested from any anomalies.

As the countdown begins, the aerospace community is poised to assess whether Starship can finally transition from experimental prototype to operational workhorse. A successful orbital flight would mark a watershed moment, validating a design that could lower the cost of access to space by an order of magnitude and enable missions that were previously deemed financially or technically infeasible. Conversely, a setback would provide valuable lessons that could refine the vehicle’s design and inform future test campaigns.

Regardless of the outcome, September 28 will be a defining day for the next chapter of space exploration. The live broadcast will allow millions to witness a pivotal experiment that could accelerate humanity’s reach beyond Earth’s gravity well, setting the stage for a new era of rapid, reusable, and far‑flung spaceflight.
